section_1.title: The Hook: The Constant Ratio
section_1.content: Introduce the concept that no matter the size of a circle, the ratio of its circumference to its diameter is always the same. Use a visual of a rolling bicycle wheel versus a giant Ferris wheel to show they share this 'secret' number.
section_1.example: If a hamster runs in a wheel with a 10cm diameter, its path length is exactly 10π cm.

section_2.title: Defining Pi (π)
section_2.content: Formal definition: π = C / d (Circumference divided by Diameter). Use an animation where a string is unwound from a circle's circumference and laid against the diameter line to show it takes exactly 3 lengths plus a small remainder (the 0.14...) to cover the distance.
section_2.example: Visualizing a pizza: slicing it into infinite thin triangles to show how the circumference relates to the radius.

section_3.title: Historical Evolution: From Estimation to Precision
section_3.content: Briefly trace history: The Ancient Babylonians used 3, the Egyptians estimated 3.16, and Archimedes used 'polygons' to trap the circle (inscribed/circumscribed). Visualize Archimedes adding more and more sides to a polygon until it 'becomes' a circle.
section_3.example: Comparing a square (4 sides) inside a circle vs. a 100-sided polygon inside a circle to show how the shape gets 'closer' to the truth.

section_4.title: The Irrational Nature of Pi
section_4.content: Explain that π is an irrational number—it never ends and never repeats. This implies that no matter how much computing power we use, we can never reach the 'end' of Pi.
section_4.example: A robot trying to memorize Pi and running out of memory capacity because the digits go on forever.

section_5.title: Summary and Real-World Relevance
section_5.content: Reiterate: Pi is the fundamental bridge between linear measurements and curved geometry. It is used today in GPS systems, space travel, and quantum physics.
section_5.example: A satellite navigation system calculating the orbit of a planet around a sun using π to ensure it doesn't crash.
